title: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
summary: How Linux ranks DRAM and CXL nodes into tiers, demotes cold pages during reclaim instead of swapping, finds hot pages trapped in slow memory and promotes them, and where zswap and SSD swap fit below.
outcomes: Explain why tiering pays off only when the hot working set is served from the fast tier
Compute a node's abstract distance and memory tier from HMAT or CDAT latency and bandwidth
Trace how reclaim demotes a cold page to CXL and what happens when migration fails
Explain how hint fault latency, the adaptive threshold and rate limits decide promotion
Estimate average access cost for a placement and diagnose thrashing from /proc/vmstat

lessons.title: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers

blocks.md:
From the CXL course you know that CXL-attached memory shows up in Linux as a **CPU-less NUMA node**: plain load/store memory, cache-coherent, but farther away than the DRAM wired to the CPU socket. This course asks what the operating system should *do* with such a node.

The motivation is cost. In Meta's TPP paper, memory is a growing share of rack cost and power, and the authors measured that **55 to 80 percent** of an application's allocated memory sits idle in any two-minute window. Paying local-DRAM prices for idle bytes is waste.

**Tiered memory** treats several kinds of memory as one hierarchy and moves pages between them by how hot they are:

- **Fast tier**: DRAM attached to the CPU socket (the *local* node).
- **Capacity tier**: CXL memory, a CPU-less NUMA node that is slower but still byte-addressable.
- **Lowest tier**: swap, either compressed in RAM by **zswap** or written to an SSD.

A page is *hot* if it is accessed often, *cold* if it is not. Moving a page to a slower tier is **demotion**; moving it back up is **promotion**.

blocks.title: The tiers and the two directions pages move

scenes.caption: The CPU reaches both DRAM and CXL memory with ordinary loads and stores. CXL is just a NUMA node with no CPUs, so no code changes are needed to use it.
When DRAM fills up, reclaim can migrate cold pages to the CXL node instead of swapping them. They stay byte-addressable; an access just costs more.
Pages that turn hot while sitting on CXL are 'trapped'. Promotion moves them back to DRAM so the hot working set is served locally.
Below CXL sits swap. zswap compresses pages into a RAM pool; when the pool hits its limit it writes the oldest entries to the SSD swap device.
The crucial difference: a page on CXL is still mapped and read in place by a load. A swapped page is unmapped, so touching it takes a page fault and a whole-page read before the load can finish.

blocks.md: How big are the gaps? The TPP paper (Figure 2) gives rough ranges: CPU-attached main memory 80 to 140 ns, CXL memory 170 to 250 ns, and SSD 10 to 40 microseconds. It summarizes CXL as adding about 50 to 100 ns over normal DRAM, similar to a remote socket on a dual-socket server. So CXL is roughly 2x DRAM, while an SSD is about 100x to 400x.

A simple model makes the stakes concrete. Let $h$ be the fraction of memory accesses served from the fast tier. If a DRAM access costs $L_f$ and a CXL access costs $L_s$, the average cost of an access that misses the CPU caches is:

blocks.caption: A first-order model: it ignores bandwidth limits, queueing, and the cost of migrating pages.

blocks.title: Average memory latency vs fraction served locally

scenes.caption: With DRAM at 100 ns and CXL at 200 ns (values inside the paper's ranges), the average falls in a straight line as more accesses hit DRAM.
TPP's Web1 workload on default Linux served only 22% of accesses locally: 0.22 x 100 + 0.78 x 200 = 178 ns. With TPP, 90% were local: 110 ns.

Slide CXL latency to 250 ns. At 22% local the average rises from 178 to 217 ns, at 90% only from 110 to 115 ns (the dots still mark the 200 ns values). Good placement makes the slow tier's speed matter less.

blocks.md: Tiering wins only if the *hot* pages live in the fast tier. The capacity of each tier matters less than the fraction of accesses it serves. Everything in this course is machinery for keeping $h$ high cheaply.

Why not let Linux handle it as a plain NUMA node? Default Linux allocates on the local node first and falls back to the CXL node when local memory is full. TPP found that whatever lands on CXL tends to stay there. In Web1, file cache filled DRAM during startup, later heap (*anonymous*) allocations spilled to CXL and stayed, and throughput dropped 16.5% versus all-local. With TPP the drop was 0.5%.

blocks.prompt: The paper ran Cache1 and Cache2 with only 1 GB of DRAM per 4 GB of CXL (a 1:4 ratio). Can any placement policy reach all-DRAM speed there?
blocks.reveal: Not if the hot working set is bigger than DRAM: the paper chose 1:4 as a stress test where only part of the hot set fits. Placement still matters a lot. For Cache1, default Linux let file cache fill DRAM, 85% of anonymous pages were trapped on CXL and throughput fell 14%. TPP promoted 97% of the hot anonymous pages within a minute by pushing less latency-sensitive file pages down. Placement chooses *which* pages get DRAM; it cannot make a hot set fit.

blocks.question: A service has 200 GB allocated, of which 40 GB is touched every few seconds and the rest is idle for minutes. Which configuration best fits tiered memory?
options: 64 GB DRAM and 160 GB CXL, with the OS demoting idle pages to CXL
160 GB DRAM and 40 GB CXL, so hot pages are guaranteed to fit
200 GB of CXL only, since CXL is cheaper per GB
64 GB DRAM and 160 GB of SSD swap, since swap is cheapest
blocks.explain: The hot 40 GB fits in 64 GB of DRAM with headroom, and idle pages go to cheaper CXL where they remain directly addressable. All-CXL puts hot data 2x farther away, and swap-only makes every access to a cold page a fault plus an SSD read.

blocks.question: Using the model with DRAM 100 ns and CXL 200 ns, what fraction of accesses must hit DRAM to get an average of 120 ns?
blocks.explain: 120 = 100h + 200(1 minus h) = 200 minus 100h, so h = 0.8. Each 1% of accesses moved to CXL adds 1 ns here.

lessons.title: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance

blocks.md: Before the kernel can demote or promote, it must know which nodes are fast and which are slow. Plain NUMA distance (the SLIT table from the NUMA course) cannot answer this: it describes how far a node is, not what kind of memory it holds. A CXL node and a remote-socket DRAM node may look equally far.

Linux groups nodes into **memory tiers** in `mm/memory-tiers.c`. Each node gets an **abstract distance** (adistance): a number where smaller means faster. Nodes whose adistance falls in the same chunk of 128 share a tier. Tiers appear in sysfs as `/sys/devices/virtual/memory_tiering/memory_tierN/nodelist`, where a smaller N is a faster tier.

Where does adistance come from? Firmware describes memory performance: ACPI **HMAT** (Heterogeneous Memory Attribute Table) for platform memory and **CDAT** (Coherent Device Attribute Table) for CXL devices. Linux exports the rated numbers per node under `/sys/devices/system/node/nodeY/access0/initiators/` as `read_latency`, `write_latency` (nanoseconds) and `read_bandwidth`, `write_bandwidth` (MiB/s). For adistance the kernel uses the numbers for the nearest CPU initiator (access class 1, under `access1/initiators/`), relative to the CPU-attached DRAM nodes:

blocks.caption: From mt_perf_to_adistance(): proportional to latency, inversely proportional to bandwidth. 576 is MEMTIER_ADISTANCE_DRAM.

blocks.md: Why 576? The header defines `MEMTIER_CHUNK_SIZE` as 128 and the DRAM default as $4 \times 128 + 64 = 576$. So default DRAM sits in the middle of chunk 4 (adistance 512 to 639) and becomes `memory_tier4`. The 64 offset lets a device that is slightly faster than DRAM still land in the same tier, and the comment in `memory_tier_init()` notes there is room for 4 faster tiers below it.

blocks.title: Mapping adistance to a memory tier (chunks of 128)

scenes.caption: Five hypothetical nodes. The reference DRAM node has read and write latency 100 ns and 100,000 MiB/s each way. We compute each node's adistance from its rated numbers (illustrative values, not a real product).
Reference DRAM: both ratios are 1, so adistance = 576, tier 576 / 128 = 4 (rounded down).
A slightly faster node (90 and 95 ns, 110,000 MiB/s each way): 576 x 185/200 = 532, then x 200,000/220,000 = 483. Chunk 384 to 511, so tier 3: a faster tier than DRAM.
CXL A at 170 ns and 64,000 MiB/s each way: 576 x 340/200 = 979, then x 200,000/128,000 = 1529. Tier 11. Note that lower bandwidth pushes it down just as much as higher latency.
CXL B (200 ns, 50,000 MiB/s) lands at 2304, tier 18. CXL C (250 ns, 30,000 MiB/s) lands at 4800, tier 37. Each distinct tier becomes one level of the hierarchy.

blocks.md:
Two rules then follow from the tier list, both in `establish_demotion_targets()`:

1. **Demotion targets**: each node demotes to the nodes of the *next lower* tier, preferring the ones with the smallest NUMA distance (ties are all kept as preferred; one is picked at random at demotion time).
2. **Top tier**: walking up from the slowest tier, the first tier that contains a node with CPUs marks the top. Every tier at or above it is top tier, and promotion only happens from lower tiers into it.

blocks.title: Demotion chain on a two-socket box with two CXL devices

scenes.caption: Both DRAM nodes compute adistance 576 and join memory_tier4. Both CXL nodes (same device type) land in memory_tier11.
Each DRAM node demotes to the lower-tier node with the smallest NUMA distance: node 0 to node 2, node 1 to node 3. Tier 4 contains CPUs, so it is the top tier.
The CXL nodes are in the lowest tier, so they have no demotion target. When they are under pressure, normal reclaim applies: swap (or zswap) or dropping clean file pages.

blocks.md: Tiers are not the same as NUMA distance. A remote-socket DRAM node is far, but it has CPUs and DRAM-class performance, so it sits in the top tier and is never a demotion target for the other socket. Only slower memory types form lower tiers.

blocks.prompt: A CXL device reports exactly DRAM's latency but half its bandwidth. Which tier does it land in?
blocks.reveal: adist = 576 x 1 x 2 = 1152, and 1152 / 128 = 9, so `memory_tier9`, a lower tier than DRAM's tier 4. The formula treats halving bandwidth exactly like doubling latency, so this device is a demotion target even though each individual access is as fast as DRAM.

blocks.question: A CXL device is onlined through the dax kmem driver, but firmware provides no HMAT or CDAT performance data. Which tier does its node join?
options: memory_tier4, the same tier as DRAM, so it is never a demotion target
memory_tier22, from the kmem default adistance of 5 x 576 = 2880
The slowest possible tier, because it has no CPUs
None: the kernel refuses to online memory without performance data
blocks.explain: drivers/dax/kmem.c starts from MEMTIER_DEFAULT_DAX_ADISTANCE (5 x 576 = 2880) and only overrides it if a performance-based algorithm can compute one. 2880 / 128 = 22.5, so tier 22. Memory onlined as ordinary system RAM instead defaults to 576 and would share tier 4 with DRAM.

blocks.question: Why does the kernel compute a single *top tier* boundary instead of letting every node promote to any faster node?
options: Because pages can only migrate between nodes in adjacent tiers
Because sysfs can only show one tier
Because the top tier is always exactly one node
Because memory near CPUs is where hot pages should end up; promoting between DRAM nodes is NUMA balancing's normal job, not tiering
blocks.explain: Tier promotion moves hot pages out of slow, CPU-less memory into memory that has CPUs. Between two DRAM nodes, ordinary NUMA balancing moves pages toward the CPU that uses them. The top-tier boundary separates the two cases (node_is_toptier()).

lessons.title: Demotion: reclaim that migrates instead of swapping

blocks.md: Recall how Linux reclaims memory. Each zone has watermarks `min`, `low` and `high`. When free pages drop below `low`, the background thread **kswapd** wakes and reclaims until free pages are back above `high`. If free pages hit `min`, allocating threads must reclaim synchronously (**direct reclaim**), which stalls them. The gap between watermarks is set by `vm.watermark_scale_factor`, default 10, meaning 0.1% of the node's memory.

Reclaim picks victims from LRU lists. Linux keeps separate lists for anonymous pages (heap, stack) and file-cache pages, each split into an *active* (recently used) and an *inactive* (candidates) list. Without tiering, an inactive anonymous page must be written to swap and an inactive clean file page is dropped.

**Demotion** changes the last step. With `/sys/kernel/mm/numa/demotion_enabled` set to 1, reclaim on a node that has a lower tier first tries to *migrate* each victim to the demotion target (`demote_folio_list()` in `mm/vmscan.c`). The page keeps its contents and stays mapped at the same virtual address; only its physical frame changes. The kernel docs for CXL say the same thing: with demotion enabled, vmscan prefers distant NUMA nodes to swap or zswap when capacity is available.

blocks.title: One reclaim pass on node 0 with demotion enabled

scenes.caption: Node 0 (DRAM) is below its low watermark. Pages A to D were used recently; E to H have not been touched since they moved to the inactive list.

kswapd scans the inactive list. E, F and G are unreferenced, so they become reclaim victims. H was referenced since the last scan, so it is spared and moved to the active list (not drawn in later scenes).
Because demotion is enabled and node 2 is node 0's target, the victims are migrated with an asynchronous page migration. No I/O, no unmapping from the process's view.
Migration to node 2 failed for G (say node 2 was full). The fallback is normal reclaim for that page: write it to swap if anonymous, drop it if it is clean file cache.
Node 0 regained three frames for new allocations. E and F are still one load away; G will cost a major page fault and an I/O if it is touched again.

blocks.md: Demotion counts as reclaim from the fast node's point of view: `nr_reclaimed += nr_demoted` in `shrink_folio_list()`. You can watch it in `/proc/vmstat` as `pgdemote_kswapd`, `pgdemote_direct`, `pgdemote_khugepaged` and `pgdemote_proactive`.

TPP added a second idea: keep **headroom** on the fast node. If kswapd stops as soon as free memory reaches `high`, a burst of new allocations (often short-lived, hot request data) quickly drives the node back below `low` and the overflow lands on CXL. TPP decouples the two decisions: reclaim keeps demoting until a higher *demotion watermark* is reached, while allocations only need the normal *allocation watermark*. In the paper this was a sysctl `demote_scale_factor` with an empirical default of 2% of node capacity.

Upstream Linux has an equivalent: a fourth watermark, `promo`, set one more gap above `high` (`setup_per_zone_wmarks()` in `mm/page_alloc.c`). When `kernel.numa_balancing` has the memory-tiering bit set, kswapd balances a node to the `promo` watermark instead of `high` (`pgdat_balanced()` in `mm/vmscan.c`), so the fast tier keeps room for promotions and bursts.

blocks.title: Free memory on a 64 GiB DRAM node versus watermarks

scenes.caption: Simplified: watermark gaps of 0.1% of 64 GiB = 16,777 pages = 65.5 MiB each (default scale factor; real min depends on min_free_kbytes). Shown above an assumed min of 100 MiB.
An allocation burst drops free memory below low. kswapd wakes.
Without tiering mode, kswapd sleeps once free memory passes high. The next burst arrives with only about 69 MiB of slack before low.
With memory tiering enabled, kswapd keeps demoting until free memory passes promo, leaving a whole extra gap of headroom for bursts and for incoming promotions.

blocks.prompt: A workload's hot set is 70 GiB, and the DRAM node is 64 GiB. You turn on demotion and the memory-tiering mode. What happens over time?
blocks.reveal: Thrashing. Reclaim must demote some hot pages because nothing colder is left, and promotion keeps pulling them back, so pages ping-pong between tiers and burn bandwidth on migration. TPP's paper warns that if the frequently accessed set exceeds the local node, aggressive reclamation will thrash hot memory across NUMA nodes. Tiering cannot fix a hot set larger than the fast tier.

blocks.md: Demotion does not follow normal memory policies. The source comment says it ignores mempolicy, and in Linux 6.15 and earlier it also ignored `cpuset.mems_allowed`. Newer kernels filter demotion targets by the cgroup's allowed nodes, but shared memory such as libc can still be demoted outside them. The sysfs ABI says not to enable it on systems that need strict cpuset placement guarantees.

blocks.question: With demotion enabled, reclaim on the DRAM node selects an inactive anonymous page and the CXL node has free space. What happens to the page?
options: It is compressed into zswap first, then moved to CXL
It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped; the process can still read it with a normal load
It is written to the swap device and its CXL copy is kept as a cache
It is dropped and re-read from disk on the next access
blocks.explain: Demotion is a page migration: same contents, new physical frame on the lower tier, page tables updated. Only if migration fails does the page fall back to ordinary reclaim (swap or zswap).

blocks.question: Why does TPP keep reclaiming past the normal high watermark on the fast node?
options: To reduce the number of pages on the CXL node
Because reclaim is cheaper when done in larger batches
To make room for short-lived hot allocations and incoming promotions so they land in DRAM instead of spilling to CXL
To keep the inactive list empty
blocks.explain: New allocations go to CXL only when the local node is short of free pages. Headroom keeps those bursts local, and promotions need free local frames too. Upstream implements this with the promo watermark.

lessons.title: Promotion: finding hot pages trapped in slow memory

blocks.md: Demotion handles cold pages in DRAM. The harder problem is the reverse: noticing that a page *on CXL* has become hot. The CPU's cache misses to CXL do not tell the kernel which pages they hit. Linux needs a cheap way to sample accesses.

The mechanism is borrowed from **NUMA balancing**. Periodically, a task's page tables are scanned and some pages are made inaccessible (set to `PROT_NONE`), by default 256 MB per scan step. The next access to such a page takes a minor fault, the **NUMA hint fault**. The handler learns which CPU touched which page, restores access, and may migrate the page. Setting `kernel.numa_balancing` to 2 (`NUMA_BALANCING_MEMORY_TIERING`) uses the same unmap-and-fault trick to place hot pages in fast memory; 3 enables both behaviors.

In tiering mode, how does a single fault tell the kernel a page is *hot*? When the scanner protects a slow-tier page it records the scan time in the page. When the fault arrives, the kernel computes the **hint fault latency**: fault time minus scan time. A hot page is touched soon after it was protected; a cold page waits a long time. Pages whose latency is below a threshold (default 1000 ms, `sysctl_numa_balancing_hot_threshold`) are promotion candidates.

blocks.title: Promoting a page from CXL via a hint fault

scenes.caption: At t = 0 ms the scanner walks the task's address space and marks a range PROT_NONE. For pages on the CXL node it also stores the scan time.
At t = 40 ms the app loads from page P. The PTE is not accessible, so the CPU raises a fault.
Latency = 40 minus 0 = 40 ms, below the 1000 ms threshold, and the promotion rate limit is not exceeded. P is a candidate.
The page is migrated to the DRAM node of the faulting CPU and the PTE is made accessible again. Future loads hit DRAM.
A second page Q, protected in the same scan, is not touched until t = 4000 ms. Its latency of 4000 ms is above threshold, so it stays on CXL.

blocks.md:
Two refinements keep this from doing harm:

- **Free space shortcut**: if the fast node has plenty of free memory (more than the `promo` watermark plus `max(1 GiB, node size / 16)`), any faulting slow page is promoted without the threshold check. For a 64 GiB DRAM node that margin is 4 GiB.
- **Rate limit**: `kernel.numa_balancing_promote_rate_limit_MBps` caps promotion per node. The default in the source is 65536 MB/s, effectively unlimited; the kernel docs suggest under one tenth of the slow memory's write bandwidth.

The threshold is not fixed. Every `numa_balancing_scan_period_max` (60,000 ms by default), `numa_promotion_adjust_threshold()` compares how many candidates appeared against what the rate limit would allow over that window, and nudges the threshold by one sixteenth of twice the default (125 ms), keeping it between 125 ms and 2000 ms.

blocks.title: Adapting the hot threshold to the rate limit

scenes.caption: Simplified from kernel/sched/fair.c. With the limit set to 1000 MB/s, the budget for one 60 s window is 256,000 x 60 = 15,360,000 candidate pages.
Window 1: 20,000,000 candidates, above the 16,896,000 upper band. The threshold tightens to 875 ms, so a page must be touched sooner after scanning to count as hot.
Window 2: 18,000,000, still above the band. Threshold 750 ms.
Window 3: 16,000,000 is inside the band (13,824,000 to 16,896,000). No change; the system has found a threshold that matches the budget.
Window 4: the workload calms to 10,000,000 candidates, below the lower band. The threshold loosens to 875 ms, and then to 1000 ms if it stays low.

blocks.md: Why so much care? TPP describes the **ping-pong** problem. Default NUMA balancing promoted a page on its first hint fault. A page touched once in a long while would be promoted, fill scarce DRAM, become the coldest page there, and be demoted again, wasting migration bandwidth in both directions. TPP's fix was to promote only pages already on the *active* LRU list: on the first fault an inactive page is just marked accessed and moved to the active list, and only a second fault promotes it. Upstream reached the same goal with the hint-fault-latency test and the adaptive threshold above.
Promotion needs two signals: *is this page hot* (recency of access) and *can we afford to move it* (free space, rate limit). Missing either one turns tiering into a migration storm.

Huge pages from the prerequisite course move as one unit. A 2 MiB THP is a single folio of 512 base pages, and the rate limiter counts all 512 (`folio_nr_pages()`). TPP also notes that production apps keep code and hot pools in pre-allocated 2 MB and 1 GB pages that should never be demoted.

blocks.prompt: In tiering mode, why does the scanner bother protecting pages that already sit on DRAM?
blocks.reveal: With mode 2 alone, it does not: the scan code skips pages on top-tier nodes when the normal NUMA balancing bit is off (`mm/mempolicy.c`). With mode 3 they are scanned again, for ordinary cross-socket balancing. TPP made the same choice, limiting sampling to CXL nodes because hint faults on local pages cost overhead with nothing to promote. Fewer protected pages means fewer minor faults on the hot path.

blocks.question: A CXL page was protected at t = 2000 ms and the app touches it at t = 3500 ms. The current threshold is 1000 ms and DRAM is nearly full. What happens?
options: It is promoted because any hint fault on a CXL page triggers promotion
It stays on CXL because its hint fault latency, 1500 ms, is not below the 1000 ms threshold
It is promoted because 3500 ms is greater than the threshold
It is demoted to swap
blocks.explain: Latency is fault time minus scan time: 3500 minus 2000 = 1500 ms, which is not below 1000 ms. Only with plenty of free DRAM (the free-space shortcut) would the threshold be skipped.

blocks.question: After you lower numa_balancing_promote_rate_limit_MBps, what does the kernel do to the hot threshold over the next windows?
options: Raises it, so more pages qualify
Lowers it step by step, so only pages touched sooner after scanning qualify
Leaves it unchanged; the rate limit only drops excess promotions
Resets it to 1000 ms every window
blocks.explain: A lower limit shrinks ref_cand. If candidates exceed 110% of that, the threshold drops by 125 ms per window (to a floor of 125 ms), so the candidate stream shrinks to match the budget instead of being cut off at random.

lessons.title: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production

blocks.md: The lowest tier is swap. Pages there are *unmapped*: an access raises a major page fault, the kernel reads the whole page back, maps it, and only then does the load complete. This is why TPP chose not to use CXL as a swap device. With swap semantics every access to a page on CXL would fault and copy a full page, pushing effective latency far above 200 ns and losing CXL's cache-line load/store access.

**zswap** sits in front of the swap device as a compressed cache in RAM. Pages being swapped out are compressed into a pool; reads that hit the pool avoid device I/O. When the pool reaches its limit (`max_pool_percent`), zswap evicts entries in LRU order to the backing swap device. Its docs note the main trade: CPU cycles for less swap I/O, which also reduces writes that wear SSDs.
How bad is an SSD access in our latency model? Extend it with a fraction $s$ of accesses that must go to SSD-backed swap at cost $L_{ssd}$:

blocks.caption: Simplified: all non-swap accesses hit DRAM at L_f = 100 ns; ignores the CPU cost of handling the fault and readahead.

blocks.title: Average access cost when a small share goes to SSD swap

scenes.caption: Baseline: every access hits DRAM at 100 ns.
One access in a thousand going to swap at 10 to 40 us (the paper's SSD range) adds 10 to 40 ns: averages of 109.9 and 139.9 ns.
At 1% the average becomes 199, 299 or 499 ns. Compare: putting 100% of accesses on 200 ns CXL gives 200 ns. A tiny swap rate can cost as much as no DRAM at all.

blocks.md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

TPP pairs well with its sibling, **TMO** (Transparent Memory Offloading). TMO runs in user space, watches memory pressure stall information, and keeps pushing reclaim so truly idle memory leaves RAM; TPP decides *which tier* the remaining pages live in. The paper calls them complementary layers: TMO removes the cold tail, TPP places the warm and hot pages.

blocks.title: TPP paper results: share of accesses served from local DRAM

scenes.caption: From the TPP paper (2:1 DRAM to CXL ratio, CXL emulated by a remote socket). Default Linux served 22% of Web1's accesses locally and 78% of Cache2's.
With TPP, local share rose to 90% and 91%. Throughput loss versus all-local fell from 16.5% to 0.5% (Web1) and from 2% to 0.4% (Cache2).

blocks.md:
A practical bring-up checklist, using only interfaces described in the kernel docs:

1. Check tiers: `cat /sys/devices/virtual/memory_tiering/memory_tier*/nodelist`. If the CXL node shares a tier with DRAM, fix firmware performance data first.
2. Enable demotion: `echo 1 > /sys/kernel/mm/numa/demotion_enabled`.
3. Enable promotion: `sysctl kernel.numa_balancing=2` (or 3 to also keep normal NUMA balancing).
4. Optionally cap promotion with `kernel.numa_balancing_promote_rate_limit_MBps`.
5. Watch `/proc/vmstat`: `pgdemote_*`, `pgpromote_success`, `pgpromote_candidate`, `numa_hint_faults`.

blocks.code:
# Is tiering doing anything?
grep -E 'pgdemote_kswapd|pgdemote_direct|pgpromote_success|pgpromote_candidate|numa_hint_faults ' /proc/vmstat

# Per-node memory use: is the hot process mostly on node 0?
numastat -p <pid>
blocks.caption: Sample twice a minute apart and compare deltas; absolute counters since boot hide the current trend.

blocks.md: Symptoms of thrashing: `pgdemote_*` and `pgpromote_success` both climbing fast at the same time. Pages are moving down and back up. Either the hot set is larger than DRAM, or headroom is too small. Migration itself consumes memory bandwidth on both tiers.

blocks.prompt: You see high `pgdemote_direct` but low `pgdemote_kswapd`. What does that suggest?
blocks.reveal: Demotion is happening mostly in **direct reclaim**: allocating threads hit the min watermark and had to demote pages themselves, adding latency to the requests that allocated. kswapd is not keeping up with the allocation rate. More headroom (a higher `watermark_scale_factor`, which also widens the promo gap) lets background reclaim start earlier.

blocks.question: DRAM holds a job's hot pages and CXL is full of warm pages touched every few seconds. Another 50 GB of pages are touched about once per hour. Where should those 50 GB go?
options: SSD swap (with zswap in front): one major fault per page per hour is negligible
Move warm CXL pages to SSD swap so the hourly pages fit on CXL
DRAM, by demoting some hot pages to CXL
Nowhere: tiering cannot help this job
blocks.explain: Cost is access rate times miss cost. An hourly page pays one 10 to 40 us fault per hour, which is nothing; a warm page on swap would fault every few seconds. The coldest pages belong in the lowest tier.

blocks.question: Why does TPP not use CXL memory as a fast swap device instead of a NUMA node?
options: Swap cannot be placed on byte-addressable memory
CXL devices do not support writes
Swap semantics turn every access into a major fault and a full-page copy, losing CXL's direct cache-line loads
The kernel cannot migrate pages to CXL
blocks.explain: The value of CXL is that warm pages can be read in place with a load at roughly 2x DRAM latency. Treating it as swap would add a fault and a 4 KiB copy to every access to a swapped page.
